name: Five in a Row
intro: Learn Five in a Row (Gomoku) from scratch: the board, making five and blocking, then threes and fours, the open four and the double threats that win games.

units.name: How Five in a Row works
units.blurb: The board, who moves first, making five and blocking.

lessons.title: The Five in a Row board and who moves first
lessons.summary: Five in a Row (Gomoku) is played on an empty 15×15 board. Learn how the board works, who moves first and where to start.
lessons.wrap: That’s the board. Next: how to win.

steps.text:
Five in a Row, also called Gomoku, is played on a 15×15 board that starts empty. Stones go on the points where the lines cross.

Players take turns placing one stone. Stones never move and are never captured.
Quick check.
steps.explain: Gold moves first. Against the computer you choose whether that’s you.

steps.text: The centre point is the classic first move: lines run out from it in every direction.
steps.done: Your first stone is down. Now it’s Ivory’s turn.

lessons.title: How to win at Five in a Row
lessons.summary: You win Five in a Row by making an unbroken line of five stones: across, down or diagonally. Practise finishing lines.
lessons.wrap: Five in any direction wins. Next: how to stop your opponent doing the same.

steps.text:
The first player to make five stones in an unbroken line wins: across, down or along either diagonal.

Here a line of six or more also counts.
You have four in a row. Ivory has blocked one end.
steps.wrong: Find the empty point that completes the line of five.
steps.done: Five in a row! You win.

steps.text: Diagonal lines count too.
steps.wrong: Look along your diagonal line of four.

lessons.title: Blocking in Five in a Row
lessons.summary: Stop your opponent before they make five: block every four at once, and block an open three before it becomes an open four.
lessons.wrap: Block fours at once and open threes straight away. Test yourself in the rules check.

steps.text: When your opponent has four in a row with an empty point at the end, they win next turn unless you block it. That comes before anything else.
Ivory has four in a row. You blocked one end earlier.
steps.wrong: Ivory still makes five next turn. Block the open end of the line.
steps.done: Blocked. Ivory can’t make five there now.

steps.text:
An open three is three in a row with both ends empty. If it isn’t blocked, it becomes an open four, with two winning points, and one stone can’t stop that.

So block an open three straight away, at one end.
Ivory has an open three.
steps.wrong: Ivory can still make an open four. Put your stone right at one end of the three.
steps.done: Blocked. Now the three can only become a four with one open end, which you can stop.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Five questions on the rules. Pass to unlock threats and tactics.

lessons.title: Five in a Row rules check
lessons.summary: Test your Five in a Row rules: who moves first, making five across, down or diagonally, and blocking fours and open threes.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the threats that win games.

steps.text: Question 1.
steps.prompt: Who moves first in Five in a Row?

steps.text: Question 2.
steps.wrong: Your four runs up and down the board. Find the open end.

steps.text: Question 3.
steps.wrong: Ivory makes five at the other end of the diagonal.

steps.text: Question 4.
steps.prompt: Ivory has four in a row with both ends empty. Can you stop it?
options: No: Ivory wins at the other end
steps.explain: An open four has two winning points and you can only block one. That’s why open threes must be blocked early.

steps.text: Question 5.
steps.wrong: Block right at one end of Ivory’s three.

units.name: Threats
units.blurb: Threes, fours, the open four and double threats.

lessons.title: Threes and fours in Five in a Row
lessons.summary: Learn the threats that drive every game of Five in a Row: the open three, the four and how each one forces a reply.
lessons.wrap: Every three and four forces a reply. Next: the open four.

steps.text:
A four threatens to make five next turn, so your opponent must block it. An open three threatens to become an open four, so it must be blocked too.

Making these threats lets you choose where your opponent plays.
You have two in a row with plenty of space around it.
steps.wrong: Add a stone to your line so it has three, with space at both ends.
steps.done: An open three. Ivory has to answer it.

steps.text: Ivory has blocked one end of your three.
steps.wrong: Extend the line at its open end so you threaten five.
steps.done: A four. Ivory must block it now.

lessons.title: The open four
lessons.summary: An open four has two winning points, so it can’t be stopped. Learn to make one from an open three your opponent missed.
lessons.wrap: An unblocked open three becomes an open four, and an open four wins.

steps.text:
Ivory didn’t block your open three. Now you can make an open four: four in a row with both ends empty.

Ivory can block one end, but you make five at the other.
Your three is open at both ends.
steps.wrong: Add a stone right next to your three, so the four has an empty point at each end.
steps.done: An open four. Whatever Ivory does, you make five next turn.

lessons.title: Double threats: four-three and three-three
lessons.summary: One stone that makes two threats at once can’t be stopped. Learn the four-three and the three-three, the moves that win most games.
lessons.wrap: Look for the point where two of your lines cross.

steps.text:
Your opponent can only block one threat per turn. So a move that makes two threats at once usually wins.

The strongest is the four-three: a four and an open three with the same stone.
Your row of three is blocked at one end, and you have two stones in a column just above it.
steps.prompt: Make a four and an open three with one stone.
steps.wrong: Find the point where your row and your column meet.
steps.done: A four-three! Ivory must block the four, and then your three becomes an open four.

steps.text: Two open twos that meet at one point.
steps.prompt: Make two open threes at once.
steps.wrong: Look for the empty point that extends both of your pairs.
steps.done: A three-three. Ivory can block only one; the other becomes an open four.

lessons.title: Stopping double threats before they happen
lessons.summary: Once your opponent has a four-three, it’s too late. Learn to spot the crossing point and take it one move earlier.
lessons.wrap: Defend the crossing points, not just the lines.

steps.text: You can’t stop a four-three once it’s made. Instead, look for the points where your opponent’s lines cross, and take them first.
Ivory’s row of three and column of two meet at one point. If Ivory plays there, it’s a four-three.
steps.prompt: Stop the double threat before it happens.
steps.wrong: Ivory still has the crossing point. Take the point where both of Ivory’s lines meet.
steps.done: Taken. Both of Ivory’s lines are now weaker.

units.name: Playing well
units.blurb: Attack first, and keep your stones together.

lessons.title: Win before you block
lessons.summary: If you can make five, do it, even when your opponent has a threat. Learn the order of priorities in Five in a Row.
lessons.wrap: Check your own winning moves before you block.

steps.text:
Every turn, check in this order:

  1. Can I make five? Do it.
  2. Can my opponent make five next turn? Block it.
  3. Can I make a four-three or an open four? Do it.
  4. Does my opponent have an open three? Block it.
Ivory has an open three, but look at your own stones first.
steps.wrong: Blocking can wait: you can win right now.
steps.done: Five in a row. Winning beats blocking.

lessons.title: Play compactly
lessons.summary: Stones close together make many possible lines; scattered stones are easy to block. Learn why strong players keep their stones together.
lessons.wrap: Keep your stones together and near the action, and look for double threats every turn.

steps.text: A stone helps you only if it can become part of a line of five. Stones close together, especially diagonally next to each other, share many possible lines. A stone far from the others shares none.
You’re choosing between two moves.
steps.prompt: Which is usually better early in the game?
options: A stone next to your group, near the centre
A stone in a far corner, away from Ivory
steps.explain: Next to your group: it joins several of your possible lines at once and gets in Ivory’s way. A distant stone builds nothing.
